editor_note: Week Two of the experiment: thirty-eight tracks pulled almost entirely from the week's editorial — Prog magazine's Tracks Of The Week, The Progspace's release roundups, The Progressive Subway's reviews, The PROG Mind, Arctic Drones on the fusion side, and the Free Jazz Collective. The idea is the old one: a magazine you can listen to. Every track below carries a note on where it came from and why it's here. No algorithms were consulted.

spotify:track:3F59wItYRllfGVIkFCBmQb.text: The Lindroth brothers' sophomore opus Ondine — "one of the most engaging and fun listens as far as Classic Melodic Prog Metal with a symphonic edge is concerned in quite some time," per The Progspace. Fusion-y synth leads, groovy riffing, and former Lost Horizon voice Daniel Heiman on top. Opening the playlist with a statement.

spotify:track:2IromxtGk6yjUf3jWp9Y8E.text: Zappa-esque satirical chaos meets virtuosic jazz fusion. The most fun find of the week — a band whose name alone earns a slot, and whose music somehow lives up to it.

spotify:track:09YtNcRsr7FR2flD9nazlY.text: From Prog's Tracks Of The Week: chiming guitars and mellifluous vocals that earned them the tag "Britain's answer to Sigur Rós." The album launch show is at The Nest, Nottingham, September 15.

spotify:track:70gMqrCiOHrmY8ICmCeS4J.text: The French quartet's latest single from November's Trame Noire — and it's a busy season: a 13-album box set celebrating twenty years drops the same day, with their 2007 debut on vinyl for the first time.
spotify:track:70gMqrCiOHrmY8ICmCeS4J.quote: "Direct and raw, the track unfolds over a relatively short span of time for an Hypno5e song… ending in a frantic chaos that announces the album's second half." — the band

spotify:track:6N7xfL2lTWRuFS2MVbAxkl.text: Cut-throat fusion with a composer's discipline — pulled from Arctic Drones' jazz-fusion roundup coverage of the Ictus sessions.

spotify:track:2UKQtt7xMDKcrE5oGkAfYV.text: A live-in-studio recording from Studio de la Fuie, ahead of second album Terminal (October 23, Klonosphere). The band on the track: about ancestors, and "bonds and interactions… more respectful of differences and more integrated into their environment."
spotify:track:2UKQtt7xMDKcrE5oGkAfYV.quote: "This track refers to ancestors and their knowledge." — Could Seed

spotify:track:00WnPNxk1Lmd1HqGmxIhqs.text: Epic doom crossed with US power metal from Canada — recommended by The Progressive Subway "for fans of Atlantean Kodex, Queensrÿche, Crimson Glory, Warlord, Lost Horizon, Fates Warning." That lineage list is a genre map all by itself.

spotify:track:76dHl6GuPUqb2Bo3SGYTzz.text: London improvisers whose Balm sessions capture the band's live telepathy on record — Satori runs nine minutes of slow-burning collective improv. Found in the Bandcamp tags, well beneath the editorial radar.

spotify:track:0PhCbeNRtuEsIMX8CYYAwv.text: Composer-led fusion from the Kimatika sessions — Arctic Drones' nu-jazz coverage keeps surfacing records that straddle composition and improvisation; this is one of them.

spotify:track:10vjuLFB9dGlq4ieIqRXdH.text: "Canada and Tech Death go together like France and wine," says The Progspace of this Quebec outfit — blistering leads, fretless bass, blast beats, and a title that translates roughly to "the stellar blaze." The second single from Theasterion.

spotify:track:4H4EmkuWdkaNcdzGyA0hzf.text: Self-titled, lowercase, lowercase track title — dijon is bedroom-recorded jazz-hop-adjacent fusion that Bandcamp's tags do better than any magazine could.

spotify:track:7I4AkS4aAugbtkKW6TXXSQ.text: Swedish post-rock lifers, twenty years in. Tree of Life is the slow-build centerpiece of And The Dead Tree Gives No Shelter — r/postrock's find, the fringe lane's gain.

spotify:track:4CW9fj0aZMtc4652Xnr7Ha.text: Indonesian djent with genuine melodic patience — The Progressive Subway's coverage of the Dove sessions flagged them as ones to watch, and the title track bears it out.

spotify:track:0Lci5APIpJjwtCt8AMLlvp.text: Newcastle jazz-punk energy with a wit most fusion forgets to bring — Carpet Doctor sounds like its title, in the best way. Held from the Week 1 pool and deployed now.

spotify:track:5z44rf6zPmfClQqfSugvXx.text: Berne's Snakeoil-adjacent chamber aggression — the Free Jazz Collective keeps the fringe lane honest, and Oddly Enough is alto-sax architecture at its most deliberate.

spotify:track:3uIzddyotvprzsfJ8e6CwM.text: Fourteen years after their debut, the Italian dark-prog metallers returned — and booked Geoff Tate (Queensrÿche) and Andy Kuntz (Vanden Plas) as guests. Weaker and Fading is the Tate duet. Semper Tacui: "I have always stayed silent."

spotify:track:77Upj6QTmlbhRqesiCYgGA.text: Warsaw noir-jazz — Niechęć means "reluctance/aversion," and Reckless Things plays like a Rybczyński film sounds: neon, rain, distrust. Nowe płuca ("new lungs") is the record breathing in.

spotify:track:0nZj6UgjZ78pYJhG36zSRU.text: Portland doom-psych on the heavier edge of the fringe lane — Spades rides a riff that would level a smaller band.

spotify:track:01XV9RtSmLIoERz6TCbuXd.text: WILDCARD. The Mega Man rock opera finally delivered Act III after seventeen years — dueling vocals, Blade Runner keys, pure Meat Loaf-scale theater. From Tennessee, of all places. The Subway's review lineup says it all: "for fans of Meat Loaf, Queen, Journey, Gunship, Dirt Poor Robins."

spotify:track:73UWmak0o1rM6SQ03Oybof.text: UK art-rockers who rang Andy Fairweather Low — "a Welsh hero," per the band — for the voice-of-reason role, and got a suitably dramatic video with it. A new EP, out now; not on the acclaimed Music Is Art — Vol. 1.
spotify:track:73UWmak0o1rM6SQ03Oybof.quote: "He is a Welsh hero. We were looking for the voice of reason, so it had to be mature." — Chimpan A

spotify:track:5MeRLYevGwkEKqpsQSsLxH.text: Guitarist's-guitarist fusion from the Convergence sessions — another Week 1 pool holdover earning its slot on phrasing alone.

spotify:track:1LgxdaKouyxqEmG1GoWWiw.text: Brussels quartet scoring silent cinema live — Assassins comes from their Pinocchio soundtrack work: post-rock with an actual pit-orchestra sense of drama.

spotify:track:0xIfYcrViPCW6lVHhRU2o2.text: UK neo-prog that pushed through considerable lineup upheaval — The PROG Mind: they "shadow-dropped their third album… and it is proving to be terrific." Linter is the tightest three minutes of it.

spotify:track:0GrPEhIDM0bdE93pfb3iI2.text: A "spectacular avant-jazz debut, driven by thrilling world-building and bold, imaginative arrangements" — Arctic Drones' own words on Philosophie du Soi. Métamorphose is the thesis statement.
spotify:track:0GrPEhIDM0bdE93pfb3iI2.quote: "A spectacular avant-jazz debut, driven by thrilling world-building and bold, imaginative arrangements." — Arctic Drones

spotify:track:08OsGYmEA6x1Af8WobsJQU.text: Pianist-composer at the head of a room-filling ensemble — Drift is exactly what the title claims, until it isn't. The Free Jazz Collective's beat keeps the fringe lane's improv credentials current.

spotify:track:7hnZg2to4y6xm3asHmJGzY.text: Colombian prog-metal, first full-length — The PROG Mind first flagged their 2024 EP and now calls Primal Repetition "head and shoulders above" it. The Same River is the calm-center showcase.

spotify:track:350t84BbIGEzTwyJZWe29A.text: Wonky, analog-worshiping fusion — the idiosyncratic capitalization is the manifesto. Pool holdover, deployed where the sequencing needed a grin.

spotify:track:3jNesgmvKCBIiQSzFKwHLB.text: Art-rock from the Somnambulist sessions — found in the tags, sleepwalking its way into the middle of Side C.

spotify:track:5V4MIrVuU5HrobVKjvodfs.text: Echoes of the Hypermind indeed — crossover prog with a metric screw loose, surfaced in The Progspace's weekly release sweep.

spotify:track:5iW8YrUo6qMtNQBTehpPeL.text: FEATURED SCENE — Zeuhl & Canterbury. National Health is the Canterbury sound at full orchestral tilt: Dave Stewart's chords, Alan Gowen's keys, and Tenemos Roads as the gateway. 1978, and still ahead of most things.

spotify:track:18HRIcxTqwNhGhISEXZM5p.text: FEATURED SCENE. Tatsuya Yoshida's volcanic Japanese zeuhl — Angherr Shisspa is maximum-prog chaos, Magma's lineage mutated through a Tokyo noise sensibility. The scene wheel's loudest stop.

spotify:track:3LTHdYIX4Fc5Rcj75EeAfM.text: FEATURED SCENE. A one-man zeuhl act out of Hong Kong — proof the Magma lineage still has strange new branches growing in places the magazines don't patrol.

spotify:track:7mnw1JkFCDGBWmUzZlixau.text: FEATURED SCENE. The other Canterbury cornerstone — 1975's The Rotters' Club, where Fitter Stoke Has A Bath turned the scene's wit into its signature. (The 30-second solo here inspired a generation of math-rockers, whatever else it did.)

spotify:track:3QQa9x8oFSE8Qulp3OMe8J.text: The former Pain of Salvation bassist's Humanised is a solo album in the fullest sense — The Almosts is its quiet, ringing center. Via The Progspace's release coverage.

spotify:track:1rixabSyd5ixNZ7l0FyL9H.text: Costa Rican multi-instrumentalist Gerardo Ruiz's project — End of a Kalpa (kalpa: an aeon in Hindu cosmology). The PROG Mind stumbled on it online and stayed. So did we.

spotify:track:5OWqeP0bdNFr1Ul2hrcBPF.text: WILDCARD. Progressive hyperpop stream-of-consciousness that shouldn't work and absolutely does — The Progressive Subway: "Style: Hyperpop, VGM, progressive rock… for fans of Knower, Danny Baranowsky, Death's Dynamic Shroud." The two wildcards this week are the edition's two most gleeful left turns.

spotify:track:1hjH6c62KSPlqfkMp4J3VY.text: FROM THE VAULT. French zeuhl-fusion, one album, 1981, then gone — Eros is its eight-minute argument for staying. Exactly the kind of record the archive lane exists to resurface.

spotify:track:2uoEFDUHqZV314Kx5Aw4S4.text: FROM THE VAULT. 1973 Italian symphonic — Zarathustra is a concept album about Nietzsche's last man, and L'ultimo Uomo is its overture in miniature. Museo Rosenbach split right after; the record didn't.

theme.name: Zeuhl & Canterbury descendants
theme.origin: Magma · Paris, 1969 — The Wilde Flowers · Canterbury, 1966
paras: This edition's spotlight bands are connected by blood, not sound. Zeuhl and Canterbury are the only two prog genres defined by family trees — who played with whom — rather than by how the music sounds.
National Health is Hatfield & The North's rhythm section starting over. Koenjihyakkei is Magma's invented language carried to Tokyo. The full lineage, member by member, is charted inside the edition.

deep.intro: The four spotlight picks — plus Dün from the vault — aren't grouped by sound at all. They're nodes on two family trees, and in these two genres, family trees ARE the genre.

trees.title: The Canterbury line · England
trees.root: The Wilde Flowers — Canterbury, 1966 · the scene's seed

items.name: Soft Machine → Matching Mole
items.note: first wave — jazz abstraction off the root

items.name: Caravan
items.note: the other first wave — pastoral, whimsical
items.art_album: In The Land Of Grey And Pink

items.name: Hatfield & The North (1975)
items.note: Phil Miller · Pip Pyle · Richard Sinclair — the scene's wit at full flower

items.name: National Health (1978)
items.note: Miller & Pyle again, + Alan Gowen of Gilgamesh — formed out of Hatfield's split, the most compositionally ambitious stop on the line

trees.caption: Same rhythm section, consecutive bands. A relay, not a coincidence.

trees.title: The zeuhl line · France → the world
trees.root: Magma — Paris, 1969 · Christian Vander invents the genre: operatic prog sung in Kobaïan (a language he made up), choir vocals over repeating bass figures

items.name: Dün (France, 1981)
items.note: one album of the Magma lineage — Eros, its eight-minute argument for staying — then gone

items.name: Koenjihyakkei (Tokyo)
items.note: Tatsuya Yoshida takes the Kobaïan language to twice the speed — Angherr Shisspa is the lineage's most volcanic modern branch

items.name: Athak (Hong Kong, now)
items.note: one-man zeuhl — proof the tree is still growing in places the magazines don't patrol

trees.caption: Zeuhl means descended from Magma's invention. That's the entire genre definition.

deep.outro: The two trees knew each other — Magma and Soft Machine toured the same early-70s European circuit and traded influence. Fifty-plus years and three continents later, both lineages are still growing. That's what this edition listens for: not a sound, but a line of descent.
paras: Zeuhl began when drummer Christian Vander formed Magma in Paris in 1969 with a science-fiction myth: the planet Kobaïa, humanity's exodus to it, and its people's language. Vander composed in that invented tongue — the genre's very name, 'zeuhl,' is a Kobaïan word. The music hits like opera run through a jazz rhythm section: massed choral voices chanting over relentless, repeating bass figures, equal parts Ellington, Bartók and sheer volume. Nobody 'sounds like' zeuhl by accident; you are zeuhl by taking up Vander's language.

Canterbury started more casually — a group of teenagers in Kent called the Wilde Flowers who splintered into Soft Machine (jazz abstraction, wild improvising) and Caravan (pastoral, whimsical song-forms). When the first wave burned out, the same players regrouped: Matching Mole from Soft Machine's ashes, then Hatfield & The North, then National Health — formed when Hatfield's guitarist Phil Miller and drummer Pip Pyle joined forces with Gilgamesh's keyboardist Alan Gowen. The music got more compositionally ambitious with each relay hand-off.

The two lines crossed early — Soft Machine and Magma shared stages on the early-70s European circuit, and each bent the other. What unites them for this edition is the membership rule: in both, a band belongs because its members descended from the source. Fifty-plus years and three continents later, both trees are still sprouting.

scene_reason: Zeuhl/Canterbury is a descent story: Magma 1969 roots through Koenjihyakkei and present-day torch-carriers; week 2 traced exactly that arc.
scene_angle: Roots to now: the French strain and the English strain, and where each line is being carried today.
